analysis.one_liner: Repeals the individual alternative minimum tax and makes the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent.
analysis.headline: The bill was never called up for a vote; it sat on the Senate calendar after its two readings in November 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the alternative minimum tax (AMT), a parallel tax originally aimed at the very top that had begun reaching more households, and would permanently lock in the lower income tax rates from 2001 and the lower capital gains and dividend rates from 2003, which were scheduled to expire. Permanent repeal and permanence for those rate cuts would reduce federal revenue by large amounts each year, with the biggest benefits going to high earners and investors. The bill was introduced on November 7, 2007, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar; no committee ever considered it and the Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income taxpayers and investors gain the most: the capital gains and dividend rate cuts in the 2003 law flow heavily to households with large investment portfolios, and making all the 2001 rate cuts permanent preserves the deepest percentage reductions at the top. Upper-middle-class households who pay the AMT would also gain from repeal. The bill provides no offsetting revenue, so the cost shows up as larger deficits.

how_it_helps.text: It sets the individual alternative minimum tax to zero for every tax year after 2006, wiping out AMT liability for affected households.

It repeals the sunset provisions of the 2001 and 2003 tax laws, making the reduced individual income tax rates and the reduced capital gains and dividend tax rates permanent instead of expiring after 2010.
It gives a one-time estimated-tax penalty safe harbor to taxpayers who owed AMT in 2006 despite having no AMT liability the year before.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury absorbs the lost revenue permanently, since the bill contains no offsetting tax increases or spending cuts; the burden ultimately falls on future taxpayers through larger deficits or on anyone relying on federal spending that would otherwise be funded. Lower- and middle-income taxpayers benefit little from the made-permanent rate cuts relative to the top, so the distribution of the tax burden shifts toward households without large investment income.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no revenue offsets, so permanent repeal of the AMT and permanent extension of the tax cuts would add large, recurring amounts to federal deficits.

The largest dollar benefits from permanently extending the capital gains and dividend rates and the 2001 rate cuts go to the highest-income households, which is why the original laws were set to expire by design rather than being made permanent.
Repealing the AMT entirely, rather than adjusting its exemptions, removes the parallel tax that serves as a backstop ensuring very high earners pay a minimum level of tax.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax relief is real for the households that pay the AMT or earn investment income, but the bill's design is one-sided: it makes every tax cut permanent and provides no way to pay for any of it, so the benefits skew heavily toward high earners and investors while the costs land on the Treasury. Fiscally, this is an expensive package with no funding mechanism, and it died without ever being debated, so no one got to weigh those trade-offs on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, read twice, and placed on the legislative calendar, and then nothing further happened before the Congress ended — no committee action, no debate, no vote.

narrative.text: Senator John Ensign introduced the bill with four Republican cosponsors on November 7, 2007.
The Senate read it a second time the next day and placed it on the calendar under General Orders, Calendar No. 476.
That was the final action; the bill never received committee consideration, debate, or a vote before the 110th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the federal government did not permanently give up the revenue from the AMT and the expiring 2001 and 2003 tax cuts; high earners and investors lost the chance at permanence, while the Treasury kept its existing revenue. Working taxpayers who pay the AMT received no relief from this bill either — no one gained on that front.

for.name: Sens. Mike Crapo, Pat Roberts, Jim Bunning, and Gordon Smith
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its original Senate cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Democratic majority
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for debate or a vote during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill never advanced in a Senate controlled by Democrats.

industries.note: This group would have gained the most from permanent capital gains, dividend, and top income tax rate cuts, and the AMT repeal; the bill's death means those cuts remained temporary and scheduled to expire. Taxpayers without large investment income would have effectively subsidized the permanence through larger deficits.

The bill would have repealed the alternative minimum tax that had been catching more middle- and upper-middle-income families each year as its thresholds failed to keep pace with incomes. They got nothing because the bill died, though Congress routinely addressed the AMT through temporary patches instead.
